title: Water Pollution Laws and Namami Gange

cards.b:
The Ganga is a standing GS3 theme. Prelims asks for dates (Ganga Action Plan, NMCG, Namami Gange) and bodies. Mains asks why clean-up has taken decades and what a better design looks like.

The water law story is also a story of institutions: boards, missions and courts.

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was the first environmental law of its kind. It was passed under Article 252, when states asked Parliament to legislate. It set up the CPCB (1974) and State Pollution Control Boards, and requires consent to establish and operate for industries.

The Water Cess Act, 1977 taxes water use by industry to fund the boards. The Environment (Protection) Act 1986 adds penalties and standards. Pollution is measured by BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) and DO (dissolved oxygen).

• Ganga Action Plan (1985): launched by Rajiv Gandhi at Varanasi; focus on sewage treatment.
  • National River Conservation Plan (1995): expanded to other rivers.
  • National Ganga River Basin Authority (2009): chaired by the PM; the Ganga was declared the National River in 2008.
  • Namami Gange (2014-15): an integrated mission with a budget of about Rs 20,000 crore for 2015-20, since extended.

The National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) is the implementing body and became an authority under the EPA in 2016.

The mission has several pillars: sewage treatment infrastructure, river-front development (ghats), river surface cleaning, afforestation, industrial effluent monitoring, biodiversity (dolphins, turtles) and public participation. The Hybrid Annuity Model and One City One Operator were used to make plants work for years.

Arth Ganga links the river to the local economy. It focuses on natural farming along banks, tourism and water use.

In M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1988) the Supreme Court ordered tanneries at Kanpur to treat effluent. In March 2017, the Uttarakhand High Court declared the Ganga and Yamuna to have the status of legal persons. The Supreme Court stayed the order. The NGT has also ordered no dumping on Ganga banks.

The polluter pays principle and precautionary principle were laid down in cases such as *Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action* (1996) and *Vellore Citizens* (1996).

The Yamuna Action Plan (since 1993) has taken large sums but the river remains highly polluted in Delhi, where most pollution comes from drains. The Jal Shakti Ministry (2019) merged water departments. Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) brings tap water to rural homes, and Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) manages groundwater with communities.

Among the issues: untreated sewage, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff, sand mining and dams that reduce flow.

Experts argue that e-flow (environmental flow) matters as much as sewage plants. A river with water and silt cleans itself, but dams and diversions cut flow. Another issue is that spending on plants did not match running costs.

The hybrid model, cleaner industry and decentralised treatment are practical fixes. Critics say progress on the ground is slow.

The Ganga basin has about 40 percent of India's people. Kanpur tanneries, Varanasi ghats and Haridwar-Rishikesh are focus points. The CPCB monitors water quality at many stations and flags polluted river stretches. Kumbh crowds create short pulses of waste. The Gangetic dolphin and the Hilsa fish are indicators of recovery.

• Water Act: 1974; CPCB: 1974.
  • Ganga Action Plan: 1985.
  • Ganga National River: 2008.
  • NGRBA: 2009; NMCG registered as a society 2011.
  • Namami Gange: 2014-15.
  • Legal person status: Uttarakhand HC, 2017 (stayed).

Prelims-style: "Which Act created the Central Pollution Control Board?" (Water Act 1974). "The Ganga Action Plan began in" (1985).

Mains-style: "Despite large expenditure, why is the Ganga still polluted? Suggest a way forward." Structure: plans and spending; reasons (sewage gap, industry, low flow, weak enforcement); Namami Gange reforms; e-flow and community role.
